topic: Induced potential, transformers and the National Grid (physics only) (HT only)
subject: physics

items.q: A straight copper rod lies horizontally between the poles of a strong magnet. Which action induces a potential difference across the ends of the rod?
items.correct: Moving the rod steadily downwards through the magnetic field
items.misconception: Holding the rod still between the poles of a strong magnet
items.why: The student pictures the magnetic field itself as the cause, so as long as the magnet is there the effect should continue. The word 'change' in the specification statement is skimmed over. The generator effect needs relative movement or a change in the magnetic field. A stationary magnet gives a steady field through the coil, nothing is changing, so no potential difference is induced.
items.random_wrong: Joining the ends of the rod with a length of copper wire

items.q: A wire is moved through a magnetic field. The two ends of the wire are not connected to anything at all. What is induced in the wire?
items.correct: A potential difference, but no current flows in the wire
items.misconception: Nothing at all, because the circuit around it is incomplete
items.why: Potential difference and current are not held apart as separate ideas, so removing one is taken to remove the other. Relative movement between a conductor and a magnetic field induces a potential difference across the ends of the conductor whatever it is connected to. A current is induced only if the conductor is part of a complete circuit.
items.random_wrong: A current, but no potential difference across the ends

items.q: The north pole of a magnet is pushed towards a coil that is part of a complete circuit. What does the magnetic field produced by the induced current do?
items.correct: It opposes the change, so it acts to repel the approaching pole
items.misconception: It reinforces the change, pulling the magnet deeper into the coil
items.why: Students expect effects to reinforce each other, and 'the coil becomes an electromagnet that attracts the magnet' feels natural. The idea of an effect that fights its own cause is unfamiliar. An induced current generates a magnetic field that opposes the original change, either the movement of the conductor or the change in magnetic field. If it reinforced the change, energy would appear from nowhere.
items.random_wrong: It strengthens the magnet's own field inside the coil, reinforcing it

items.q: A student pushes a magnet into a coil that is part of a complete circuit. Why must the student do work to keep the magnet moving inwards?
items.correct: An induced magnetic field pushes back on the moving magnet
items.misconception: The induced magnetic field attracts the magnet, so it must be held back
items.why: Students expect effects to reinforce each other, and 'the coil becomes an electromagnet that attracts the magnet' feels natural. The idea of an effect that fights its own cause is unfamiliar. An induced current generates a magnetic field that opposes the original change, either the movement of the conductor or the change in magnetic field. If it reinforced the change, energy would appear from nowhere.
items.random_wrong: Friction in the coil's windings resists the magnet as it moves in

items.q: A coil is rotated between the poles of a magnet. Which change would increase the size of the potential difference induced in the coil?
items.correct: Winding more turns onto the coil and then rotating it faster
items.misconception: Using thicker copper wire of lower resistance for the coil
items.why: Resistance has dominated every electricity topic so far, so the student reaches for it as the controlling factor here too. The induced potential difference depends on how fast the magnetic field through the coil changes and on the number of turns. The wire's resistance affects the current only after a potential difference has been induced.
items.random_wrong: Holding the coil still in the strongest part of the field

items.q: A north pole is pushed into a coil and the meter needle flicks to the right. Which change would make the needle flick to the left instead?
items.correct: Pulling the same north pole straight back out of the coil
items.misconception: Pushing the same north pole in far more quickly than before
items.why: The size factors and the direction factors are learned as one undifferentiated list, so any change is assumed to change everything. Speed, field strength and the number of turns change only the size. Only reversing the direction of the movement or reversing the poles of the magnet reverses the direction.
items.random_wrong: Winding many more turns of wire onto the same coil

items.q: A magnet is pushed into a coil connected to an ammeter, held completely still inside the coil for two seconds, and then pulled out. What does the ammeter read while the magnet is held still?
items.correct: Zero, because the field through the coil is not changing
items.misconception: A steady current, because the magnet's field is inside the coil
items.why: The student pictures the magnetic field itself as the cause, so as long as the magnet is there the effect should continue. The word 'change' in the specification statement is skimmed over. The generator effect needs relative movement or a change in the magnetic field. A stationary magnet gives a steady field through the coil, nothing is changing, so no potential difference is induced.
items.random_wrong: A reversed current, because stopping the magnet flips its direction

items.q: A wire is moved downwards between the poles of a magnet, and then moved upwards at twice the speed. Compared with the downward movement, the potential difference induced during the upward movement is:
items.correct: twice the size, in the opposite direction
items.misconception: twice the size, in the same direction as before
items.why: The student attends to the motion and ignores the direction of the magnetic field, treating a magnet as a single object rather than as a field with a direction. Reversing the poles reverses the direction of the magnetic field through the coil, so the induced potential difference and induced current reverse as well.
items.random_wrong: the same size, but in the opposite direction

items.q: An alternator and a dynamo are both turned steadily by the same motor. How do their outputs differ?
items.correct: The alternator generates ac, while the dynamo generates dc
items.misconception: The dynamo generates ac and the alternator generates dc
items.why: The pair is memorised as a bare fact with no reason attached, so it is easy to swap. Bicycle dynamos are also often ac in real life, which muddies the memory further. The name is the clue and the hardware is the reason: an alternator has slip rings and alternates, while a dynamo has a split-ring commutator that swaps the connections every half turn so the output stays in one direction.
items.random_wrong: Both generate ac, though the dynamo's output is larger

items.q: A dynamo and an alternator have identical coils and magnets. Which part of the dynamo makes its output a direct current?
items.correct: A split-ring commutator, which swaps the connections every half turn
items.misconception: A pair of slip rings, which keep the coil joined to the same contacts
items.why: Slip rings and commutators look similar in diagrams, and the student remembers that a generator has rings without recording which kind does what. Slip rings keep the connections fixed, so the output alternates: that is the alternator. The split ring swaps the connections every half turn, so the output stays one way: that is the dynamo.
items.random_wrong: A commutator that holds the output at one steady value

items.q: Which describes the graph of potential difference generated in the coil against time for a dynamo turning steadily?
items.correct: A series of humps that never cross below the time axis
items.misconception: A straight horizontal line at one constant positive value
items.why: 'Direct current' has always been illustrated with the steady output of a cell, so students equate dc with constant. Direct current means the direction never reverses; it does not mean the size is constant. A dynamo's output rises and falls as the coil turns but never crosses the time axis.
items.random_wrong: A wave that rises and falls equally either side of the axis

items.q: The coil of an alternator is turned twice as fast as before. How does the graph of potential difference against time change?
items.correct: The peaks are taller and closer together
items.misconception: Just as tall as before, but the peaks are spaced further apart
items.why: The student transfers the idea of frequency from wave topics, where changing frequency need not change amplitude, and forgets that here the speed of rotation also sets how fast the field through the coil changes. Turning the coil faster makes the magnetic field through it change faster, so the induced potential difference is larger as well as more frequent. Both the height and the spacing of the peaks change.
items.random_wrong: The peaks are closer but no taller than before

items.q: How does a microphone make use of the generator effect?
items.correct: Pressure variations in a sound wave are converted into variations in current
items.misconception: Variations in current are converted into pressure variations in the air
items.why: Microphones and loudspeakers are built from the same parts and are taught together, so their two directions of energy transfer get exchanged. A loudspeaker uses the motor effect, turning a varying current into movement and sound. A microphone works the other way, using the generator effect to convert the pressure variations in sound waves into variations in current.
items.random_wrong: Sound shakes the magnet to and fro inside a coil that stays fixed

items.q: A sound wave reaches the diaphragm of a moving-coil microphone. What happens next?
items.correct: The diaphragm and its coil vibrate near a magnet, inducing a current
items.misconception: The diaphragm makes the magnet vibrate inside a coil that is fixed
items.why: In classroom demonstrations of induction it is always the magnet that is pushed into the coil, so that picture is carried across even though the device is named after its moving coil. In a moving-coil microphone the pressure variations move the diaphragm and the coil fixed to it. The coil moves relative to the magnet's field, which is what induces the varying potential difference.
items.random_wrong: A current in the coil makes the diaphragm vibrate and give out a sound

items.q: What does a basic transformer consist of?
items.correct: A primary coil and a secondary coil wound on an iron core
items.misconception: A primary coil and a secondary coil joined by a copper wire
items.why: The core is drawn as a solid metal loop connecting the coils, which looks exactly like a conducting path in a circuit diagram. The two coils are not joined electrically. The core carries a changing magnetic field, not a current, and it is that changing field through the secondary coil that induces a potential difference.
items.random_wrong: Two coils wound on a solid copper core so charge passes easily across

items.q: Why is the core of a basic transformer made of iron?
items.correct: Iron is easily magnetised by the changing field
items.misconception: Iron conducts an electric current better than copper
items.why: Metal in a circuit diagram means conductor to most students, and iron's magnetic behaviour is not the property they reach for first. The core's job is magnetic, not electrical. Iron is easily magnetised, so the changing field made by the primary coil is carried strongly through to the secondary coil.
items.random_wrong: Iron carries the current across from one coil to the other

items.q: Which statement correctly links the potential differences and the numbers of turns on the two coils of a transformer?
items.correct: Vp / Vs = np / ns, so the ratio of the pds equals the ratio of the turns
items.misconception: Vp / Vs = ns / np, so the ratio of the pds is the inverse turns ratio
items.why: The ratio is remembered as a formula with no physical anchor and is written upside down, and the idea of a fixed amount being 'shared out' is borrowed from series circuits. Write the equation exactly as the specification gives it: Vp / Vs = np / ns. More turns on the secondary makes Vs larger than Vp, which is a step-up transformer.
items.random_wrong: Vp + Vs = np + ns, so the pds and the turns must add up to match

items.q: A transformer has 40 turns on its primary coil and 800 turns on its secondary coil. The potential difference across the primary coil is 15 V. What is the potential difference across the secondary coil?
items.why: The ratio is remembered as a formula with no physical anchor and is written upside down, and the idea of a fixed amount being 'shared out' is borrowed from series circuits. Write the equation exactly as the specification gives it: Vp / Vs = np / ns. More turns on the secondary makes Vs larger than Vp, which is a step-up transformer.
items.random_wrong: 300 watts

items.q: A transformer has 1200 turns on its primary coil, 60 turns on its secondary coil, and a primary potential difference of 240 V. Which describes this transformer and its secondary potential difference?
items.correct: Step-down, and the secondary potential difference is 12 V
items.misconception: Step-up, and the secondary potential difference becomes 4800 V
items.why: The ratio is remembered as a formula with no physical anchor and is written upside down, and the idea of a fixed amount being 'shared out' is borrowed from series circuits. Write the equation exactly as the specification gives it: Vp / Vs = np / ns. More turns on the secondary makes Vs larger than Vp, which is a step-up transformer.
items.random_wrong: Step-down, and the secondary pd is only 0.2 V

items.q: Which units belong with the quantities in the transformer equations?
items.correct: Potential difference in volts, V; power in watts, W
items.misconception: Potential difference in watts, W; and power in volts, V
items.why: The symbol V is used both for the quantity potential difference and for the unit volt, and the letter W is read as a word beginning 'watt' or 'work', so the pairs get crossed. Potential difference is always measured in volts, V, and power is always measured in watts, W. Multiplying volts by amperes gives watts.
items.random_wrong: Potential difference in watts, W; power in amperes, A

items.q: A transformer is described as 100% efficient. What does this tell you about its coils?
items.correct: The power output at the secondary equals the power input at the primary
items.misconception: The current in the secondary coil equals the current in the primary coil
items.why: Conservation of current in a series circuit is a firmly held rule, and the two coils are wrongly pictured as one circuit. The coils form two separate circuits. What is shared is the power: Vs × Is is the power output and Vp × Ip is the power input, and only these products are equal.
items.random_wrong: The secondary coil delivers more power than the primary takes in

items.q: A transformer that can be treated as 100% efficient supplies 24 W to a lamp from a 230 V mains supply. What current is drawn from the input supply?
items.why: V = I R is applied without noticing that the two coils are separate circuits, so 'more volts means more amps' is carried straight across. For a 100% efficient transformer Vs × Is = Vp × Ip. If Vs is ten times Vp then Is must be a tenth of Ip, so stepping the potential difference up steps the current down.

items.q: Why is electrical power transmitted across the National Grid at a very high potential difference?
items.correct: A high pd means a small current, so less energy heats the cables
items.misconception: A high pd lowers the resistance of the cables, so less energy is wasted
items.why: Any explanation involving wasted heat is attached to resistance, and students assume the applied potential difference can change it. The cables' resistance is fixed by what they are made of and how long they are. The high potential difference works by cutting the current, and the heating effect depends on the current in the cables.
items.random_wrong: A high pd drives a large current, which carries the power to homes faster

items.q: Why must the supply connected to the primary coil of a transformer be an alternating current?
items.correct: Only a changing current gives a changing field in the core
items.misconception: A direct current cannot pass along the wire of the primary coil at all
items.why: The rule 'transformers only work with a.c.' is remembered as 'd.c. cannot get through a transformer'. The absence of an output is transferred back to the input, so the coil is imagined as a barrier that physically stops direct current. Direct current passes through the primary coil perfectly well, since the coil is a continuous conductor. It creates a steady magnetic field in the core, and a field that is not changing induces no potential difference in the secondary. The transformer fails to give an output, not to carry a current.
items.random_wrong: An alternating current can jump the gap between the two coils

items.q: A power station transformer has 500 turns on the primary and 25 000 on the secondary. The primary coil takes 8000 A at 25 kV. What is the current in the secondary coil?
items.why: The ratio is remembered as a formula with no physical anchor and is written upside down, and the idea of a fixed amount being 'shared out' is borrowed from series circuits. Write the equation exactly as the specification gives it: Vp / Vs = np / ns. More turns on the secondary makes Vs larger than Vp, which is a step-up transformer.

items.q: A grid link transfers 200 MW. Transformers raise the transmission potential difference from 25 kV to 400 kV. What is the current in the cables now?
items.why: The symbol V is used both for the quantity potential difference and for the unit volt, and the letter W is read as a word beginning 'watt' or 'work', so the pairs get crossed. Potential difference is always measured in volts, V, and power is always measured in watts, W. Multiplying volts by amperes gives watts.

items.q: A coil is connected to a sensitive ammeter and there is no cell in the circuit. Can a current flow?
items.correct: Yes. Moving a magnet near the coil induces a potential difference across the coil, and because the circuit is complete a current is induced.
items.misconception: A moving wire has a current induced in it directly, because its motion through the field drives a current.
items.why: Every circuit a student has built before this topic contains a cell, and 'the cell pushes the charge round' has been the working rule for years. Nothing in that rule prepares them for a source of potential difference that is a piece of moving metal. The generator effect is itself a source of potential difference. Relative movement between a conductor and a magnetic field, or a change in the magnetic field around a conductor, induces a potential difference across the ends of the conductor, with no cell needed.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why does a bicycle with its dynamo switched on feel harder to pedal?
items.correct: The induced current makes a magnetic field that opposes the rotation, so more work must be done to keep the coil turning.
items.misconception: It only feels harder because of ordinary friction in the dynamo's bearings and gears.
items.why: Friction is the student's default explanation for anything that resists motion, and the magnetic opposition is invisible. The opposing force is magnetic, not frictional. Because the induced current's field opposes the change, work must be done against it, and that work is what becomes the electrical energy delivered by the generator.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a step-up transformer increase the power delivered?
items.correct: No. If the transformer were 100% efficient, the power output would equal the power input.
items.misconception: Yes, stepping up the potential difference steps up the power as well.
items.why: 'Step up' sounds like a general increase, and students rarely separate potential difference from power. A transformer changes the potential difference and the current together. Vs × Is = Vp × Ip, so a larger secondary potential difference goes with a smaller secondary current, and no extra power is created.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Would a transformer work if its primary coil were connected to a battery?
items.correct: No. A steady direct current gives a steady magnetic field, so nothing is induced in the secondary coil.
items.misconception: Yes, it would work in just the same way, because a battery still drives a current through the primary.
items.why: The student sees the primary current as the thing that matters and does not notice that it is the change in the field, not the field itself, that induces a potential difference. Only a changing magnetic field induces a potential difference. An alternating current in the primary coil keeps the field in the core changing, which is why transformers need an alternating supply.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a high transmission potential difference mean a high current in the cables?
items.correct: No. For a fixed power transfer, raising the potential difference lowers the current.
items.misconception: Yes, a high potential difference pushes a large current along the cables, which is how so much power is delivered.
items.why: 'High voltage' and 'high current' are treated as the same idea of a powerful supply, and the fixed product V × I is not brought to mind. Power equals potential difference multiplied by current. If the power transferred is fixed, the two quantities trade off: a very high potential difference goes with a very small current.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does adding more turns to a coil change the potential difference induced in it?
items.correct: Yes. More turns on the coil gives a larger induced potential difference.
items.misconception: The number of turns makes no difference, since the magnet and its field have not changed.
items.why: The student focuses entirely on the magnet as the active object and treats the coil as a passive piece of wire. The number of turns is one of the factors that affect the size of the induced potential difference, along with the speed of the relative movement and the strength of the magnetic field.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
